# Adjudication Task — Chapter 689

## Korean source

```text
  1|＃689화
  2|
  3|
  4|
  5|툭. 투둑.
  6|
  7|차갑다.
  8|
  9|그것이 눈을 뜬 요희가 떠올린 첫 생각이었다.
 10|
 11|그리고 멍하니 이마 위로 떨어지는 물방울을 바라보던 그녀의 뇌리에, 잠시 잊고 있던 기억들이 하나둘씩 떠올랐다.
 12|
 13|‘이건.’
 14|
 15|이제야 기억난다. 자신이 누구인지. 어떤 삶을 살았는지. 요서부에서 무슨 일이 있었으며, 독혈지에서 무엇을 보았는지.
 16|
 17|그리고…….
 18|
 19|
 20|
 21|‘사랑하오, 요희.’
 22|
 23|
 24|
 25|떠올리는 것만으로도 몸서리쳐지는 어느 사내의 얼굴과 목소리. 그의 뒤에 쓰러져 있는 거대한 백호와 한 청년의 모습.
 26|
 27|그 모든 것들이.
 28|
 29|“흡……!”
 30|
 31|번개처럼 상체를 일으킨 요희는 입술 사이로 뛰쳐나오려는 비명을 간신히 삼켰다.
 32|
 33|마침내 쓰러지기 전의 기억을 모두 떠올린 그녀는, 경계심과 두려움에 사로잡혀 주위를 둘러보았다.
 34|
 35|‘이곳은 어디지?’
 36|
 37|알 수 없는 공간이었다. 흐릿한 어둠과 주위에 내려앉은 적막. 이렇다 할 빛이 없어 모든 것을 제대로 분간할 수는 없지만, 사방이 가로막혀 있다는 것만은 확실했다.
 38|
 39|마치 누군가 준비한 감옥처럼.
 40|
 41|‘흑웅.’
 42|
 43|아니, 흑웅이라는 이름을 훔친 자.
 44|
 45|삶 자체가 거짓이었던 사내를 떠올린 요희는 본능적으로 허리춤을 더듬었다.
 46|
 47|만일을 대비하여 언제나 요대처럼 두르고 다니던 연검(軟劍)을 찾기 위해서였지만, 그녀의 바람과는 달리 손에 닿는 것은 피와 흙으로 젖은 비단뿐이었다.
 48|
 49|‘아. 그때.’
 50|
 51|정체 모를 약에 취해 연검을 놓쳤던 것이 기억났다.
 52|
 53|처음부터 해약(解藥)을 복용하지 않았으니, 당연히 공력도 여전히 금제되어 있는 상태…….
 54|
 55|“어?”
 56|
 57|자신도 모르게 소리를 흘린 요희는 황급히 입을 틀어막았다. 하지만 숨기지 못한 놀라움은 동그랗게 뜨인 눈에 고스란히 드러났다.
 58|
 59|‘어떻게?’
 60|
 61|애써 마음을 가라앉힌 요희는 혹시나 하는 마음에 두 번, 세 번에 걸쳐 자신의 몸을 파악했고, 이내 확신할 수 있었다.
 62|
 63|‘공력의 금제가…… 풀려 있어.’
 64|
 65|그건 틀림없는 사실이었다. 온갖 영약을 섭취하며 축적한 공력이 하단전에 충만한 것을 느낄 수 있었으니까.
 66|
 67|문제는 왜, 그리고 어떻게라는 의문이었다.
 68|
 69|‘나를 비롯한 모두가 흑웅에게 사로잡혔을 텐데.’
 70|
 71|요희로서는 도무지 이해할 수 없는 상황이었다.
 72|
 73|이 밀폐된 공간에 홀로 남겨져 있는 것도, 금제가 풀려 있는 것도.
 74|
 75|분명 마지막 순간, 흑웅을 막을 수 있는 것은 아무도 없었다.
 76|
 77|상당한 중상을 입은 진태경은 최소 며칠간은 깨어나지 못할 상태였고, 능히 절정 고수 한 사람의 몫을 해내는 영물인 백호는 불의의 기습으로 목숨이 경각에 달해 있었으니까.
 78|
 79|단환의 영향으로 검 한번 휘둘러 보지 못한 채 쓰러진 그녀는 말할 것도 없다.
 80|
 81|‘그런데 어떻게 금제가 풀린 상태일 수 있지?’
 82|
 83|심지어 그 흔한 밧줄이나 쇠사슬로 포박당해 있던 것도 아니다. 비록 요희의 무공이 높은 편이 아니라고는 해도 절정 초입의 경지.
 84|
 85|이건 암천의 소행이라 보기에는 너무나도 어설프고, 이상한 조치였다.
 86|
 87|‘혹시.’
 88|
 89|마른침과 함께 뒷말을 삼킨 요희는 조심스럽게 자리에서 일어나 주위를 자세히 살폈다.
 90|
 91|그사이 어둠에 익숙해진 눈과 공력이 더해지자, 향상된 안력(眼力)은 어둠 너머의 광경을 읽어 냈다.
 92|
 93|‘이건…….’
 94|
 95|그리고 자신이 서 있는 공간의 정체를 확인한 순간, 요희는 숨이 턱 막히는 것을 느꼈다.
 96|
 97|거대한 공간이었다. 한 사람을 가두기 위해 만들어졌다고는 믿을 수 없는.
 98|
 99|그러나 단지 넓기만 했다면 지금처럼 숨이 막히지는 않았을 것이다. 얼핏 짐작해도 반경 수백여 장에 달할 것 같은 면적은 중요하지 않다.
100|
101|문제는 차갑고 축축한 암석이 바닥부터 벽. 그리고 천장까지 사방을 감싸고 있다는 것이었다.
102|
103|마치 누구도 출입할 수 없는 철옹성처럼.
104|
105|‘이곳은 도대체.’
106|
107|요희가 주위를 가득 메운 암석과 그 위를 뒤덮은 굵은 넝쿨을 바라보며 할 말을 잃은 순간이었다.
108|
109|솨아아아.
110|
111|어디선가 불어온 바람에 넝쿨이 흔들렸다.
112|
113|입을 벌린 채 전신을 스치는 서늘한 바람을 맞던 요희는, 문득 머리 위로 떨어져 내리는 무언가를 느끼고 손을 뻗었다.
114|
115|스륵. 툭.
116|
117|가느다란 손가락 사이에 잡힌 무언가.
118|
119|섬단 같은 머리카락을 스치며 떨어져 내린 그것의 정체는 넝쿨에서 떨어져 나온 잎사귀였다.
120|
121|독혈지에서 봤던 것과는 달리, 생명력으로 충만한 푸른 잎사귀.
122|
123|바로 그때였다.
124|
125|멍하니 그것을 내려다보던 요희의 뇌리에, 한 줄기 벼락이 스쳐 지나간 것은.
126|
127|‘잠깐. 바람?’
128|
129|밀폐된 공간이라면 바람이 불 수 없다. 이건 봉쇄되어 있지 않은 틈새가 있다는 뜻이다.
130|
131|그것도 저 굵은 넝쿨들을 흔들 정도의 강한 바람이 불어올 만큼 커다란 틈새가.
132|
133|그러나 요희의 짐작과 달리, 아무리 찾아보아도 틈새는 찾아볼 수 없었다.
134|
135|‘이럴 리가 없는데.’
136|
137|사방을 가로막은 암석을 만져도 보고, 공력을 실어 후려치기도 했다.
138|
139|그뿐인가. 혹시나 하는 마음에 익혀 본 적도 없던 벽호공(壁虎功)을 따라 하여 넝쿨을 타고 올라가기까지 했다.
140|
141|저 위에 이곳을 탈출할 수 있는 틈새가 있을까 싶어서.
142|
143|하지만 결국 모든 시도는 수포로 돌아갔다.
144|
145|이제는 암천에 의해 사로잡혔다는 절망감이 아닌, 이해할 수 없는 공간에 들어왔다는 막막함이 들 정도로.
146|
147|‘하다못해 출구도 없다는 건 말이 안 돼.’
148|
149|말 그대로였다. 깨어난 직후 어림잡아도 두 시진이 넘는 시간을 헤맨 요희였지만, 틈새는 고사하고 출구 비슷한 것도 찾지 못했다.
150|
151|그럼 누가, 어떻게 자신을 이곳에 가뒀단 말인가.
152|
153|망연자실해진 요희는 털썩 주저앉아 석벽에 등을 기댔다. 등을 타고 전해지는 따뜻하고 푹신한 감촉에 기분이 한결 나아졌다.
154|
155|“응?”
156|
157|뭔가 이상한데.
158|
159|잠시 눈을 깜빡이던 요희는 기댄 자세 그대로 슬그머니 뒷목을 젖혔다.
160|
161|그리고 흐릿한 어둠 속에서 자신을 내려다보는 청백색 눈동자와 시선이 마주쳤다.
162|
163|“아.”
164|
165|- 크릉.
166|
167|순간 내려앉은 숨 막히는 침묵.
168|
169|천천히 몸을 일으킨 요희는 자신의 등 뒤에 절벽처럼 자리 잡은 암벽과 뭔가에 잘린 듯 상반신만 불쑥 튀어나와 있는 거대한 백호를 번갈아 바라봤다.
170|
171|그리고 생각했다.
172|
173|‘뭐지 이거.’
174|
175|요희는 애써 침착하게 현재 상황을 정리했다.
176|
177|첫째. 이곳은 정체를 알 수 없는 거대한 공간이다.
178|
179|둘째. 마치 절벽 안에 갇힌 것처럼 하늘까지 암벽에 가로막혀 있고, 출구도 보이지 않는다.
180|
181|셋째. 그 암벽에서 몸통이 반쯤 잘린 백호가 나타났다. 아니, 갑자기 솟아났다.
182|
183|넷째. 이런 상황에서 답은 둘 중 하나다.
184|
185|꿈. 아니면 저승.
186|
187|요희는 망설임 없이 암벽에 머리를 박았다.
188|
189|쿵.
190|
191|골이 울리는 와중에도 깨지 않는 걸 보면 후자가 틀림없었다.
192|
193|그도 그럴 것이, 유령처럼 상반신만 둥둥 떠 있는 저 백호의 모습은 제법 낯이 익었으니까.
194|
195|‘쟤, 걔잖아.’
196|
197|은빛이라 불러도 될 만큼 새하얀 털에 청백색 눈동자.
198|
199|틀림없다. 소궁주 야율목이 애지중지하는 그 백호가.
200|
201|이미 죽었어야 할 무야호가 다친 곳 하나 없이 멀쩡히, 그리고 천연덕스럽게 고개를 갸우뚱거리는 모습에 요희는 이곳이 저승이라는 걸 확신했다.
202|
203|‘어쩐지 출구가 없더라니.’
204|
205|몰랐다. 저승은 처음이라서.
206|
207|잔뜩 꼬여 있던 실타래가 풀리는 듯한 기분. 마침내 찾아온 깨달음과 함께 요희의 어깨가 들썩이기 시작했다.
208|
209|“흑. 흐윽. 흑웅 이 씨이발 새끼…….”
210|
211|남만에 닥친 위기? 요족의 대족장으로서 지켜야 할 체면?
212|
213|그게 무슨 상관인가. 이미 죽어 버렸는데.
214|
215|지금 그녀를 지켜보는 시선이라고는 반 토막 난 호랑이 유령밖에 없다.
216|
217|거기에 더해 이십 년 전 돌아가신 어머니까지 떠올리니 눈물이 줄줄 흘렀다.
218|
219|“흐억. 흐어어어엉!”
220|
221|흡사 맹수의 포효와도 같은 울음소리에, 혹시 동족이었나 하는 표정으로 요희를 바라보던 무야호가 다가와 눈물을 핥아 주었다.
222|
223|- 크르릉.
224|
225|얼굴 전체를 쓸어올리는 까슬까슬한 촉감.
226|
227|이미 유령이 된 것치고는 너무 감각이 생생한 거 아닌가 싶었지만, 생각해 보면 죽은 뒤 감각이 없어진다는 이야기도 저승 안 가 본 놈들이나 하던 소리다.
228|
229|요희는 무야호의 푹신한 털에 얼굴을 파묻고 엉엉 울었다.
230|
231|적어도 부드럽고 살랑거리는 무언가가 손에 잡히기 전까지는.
232|
233|덥석.
234|
235|- 하악.
236|
237|처음에는 우느라 신경도 안 썼고, 그다음에는 이게 뭔가 싶었다.
238|
239|그리고 무야호가 토해 낸 날 선 울음소리에 고개를 들었을 때, 요희는 볼 수 있었다.
240|
241|자신의 손에 잡힌 길고 새하얀 백호의 꼬리를.
242|
243|‘뭐야, 꼬리였네. 난 또 뭐라고.’
244|
245|내심 중얼거린 요희는 다시 털 사이에 얼굴을 묻었고, 잠시 후 다시 고개를 들었다.
246|
247|뒤통수를 후려친 한 가지 충격적인 사실 때문이었다.
248|
249|‘잠깐. 꼬리가 왜 있어.’
250|
251|평상시라면 하등 이상할 것 없는 일이었다. 평범한 호랑이도, 심지어는 요서부 곳간에 득실거리던 쥐새끼들에게도 꼬리는 달려 있었으니까.
252|
253|그러나 조금 전만 해도 상체만 둥둥 떠다니던 백호 유령이 완전체로 거듭났다는 것은, 요희에게 있어 완전히 다른 이야기였다.
254|
255|‘설마?’
256|
257|황급히 자리에서 일어난 요희가 무야호가 처음 모습을 드러냈던 암벽을 향해 손을 뻗었다.
258|
259|탁.
260|
261|지금껏 살펴본 바와 같이 차갑고 단단하다. 두께를 짐작할 수도 없고 틈새 따위는 보이지도 않는다.
262|
263|하지만 실망하기에는 일렀다.
264|
265|‘내가 모르는 뭔가가 있어. 분명히.’
266|
267|침착함을 되찾은 이성이 말하고 있었다.
268|
269|여기는 꿈속도, 저승도 아니라고. 단지 사람의 머리로 쉽게 이해할 수 없는 기기묘묘(奇奇妙妙)한 상황일 뿐이라고.
270|
271|그리고 이러한 요희의 생각을 읽은 것처럼, 그녀의 주위를 맴돌던 무야호가 움직이기 시작했다.
272|
273|- 그르릉.
274|
275|낮은 울음소리를 흘린 거대한 백호가 하체를 비스듬히 굽힌다.
276|
277|맑은 청백색 눈동자에 담긴 뜻을 어렴풋이 알아차린 요희가 설마 하는 표정으로 물었다.
278|
279|“타라는 거니? 네 등에?”
280|
281|- 크릉.
282|
283|“하.”
284|
285|영특하다고는 들었지만, 이 정도일 줄이야.
286|

An impregnable fortress with no way in or out.

[P47]
*What in the world is this place?*

[P48]
Yohi was staring at the stone and the thick vines spread across it when a wind blew from somewhere.

[P49]
Swoooosh.

[P50]
The vines swayed. Yohi stood with her mouth open, letting the cool air wash over her. Something fell from above, and she reached out.

[P51]
Rustle. Tap.

[P52]
She caught it between her fingers.

[P53]
It was a leaf from one of the vines, fallen past her silky hair. Unlike the leaves she had seen in the Poisonblood Grounds, it was green and full of life.

[P54]
Then a realization struck her.

[P55]
*Wait. Wind?*

[P56]
Wind could not blow through a sealed space. There had to be an opening—and one large enough to let in a gust that could shake those thick vines.

[P57]
Yet search as she might, Yohi could find no gap.

[P58]
*That can’t be right.*

[P59]
She felt along the stone surrounding her, then struck it with internal energy. She even tried imitating the Wall Lizard Technique, which she had never learned, and climbed the vines in case there was an opening overhead.

[P60]
Every attempt came to nothing.

[P61]
She had stopped despairing over being captured by Dark Heaven. Now she was simply at a loss in a place she could not understand.

[P62]
*There has to be an exit, at least.*

[P63]
More than two shichen had passed since she woke, and she had spent that time searching. She had found nothing resembling an exit, let alone a gap.

[P64]
Then who had put her here? And how?

[P65]
Yohi sank to the ground and leaned against the stone wall. Warmth and softness met her back, making her feel a little better.

[P66]
“Hm?”

[P67]
Something was wrong.

[P68]
She blinked, then slowly tipped her head back without moving away.

[P69]
A pair of blue-white eyes looked down at her through the dimness.

[P70]
“Ah.”

[P71]
—Grrr.

[P72]
A suffocating silence fell.

[P73]
Yohi rose slowly, looking from the cliff-like wall behind her to the massive White Tiger protruding from it. Only its upper body showed, as though the rest had been cut away.

[P74]
*What is this?*

[P75]
She tried to take stock of the situation.

[P76]
First, she was in an enormous place she knew nothing about.

[P77]
Second, stone blocked even the sky, as though she were trapped inside a cliff. There was no visible exit.

[P78]
Third, a White Tiger with half its body missing had appeared from the wall. No—it had suddenly sprung out of it.

[P79]
Fourth, there were only two possible explanations.

[P80]
A dream. Or the afterlife.

[P81]
Yohi slammed her head against the wall.

[P82]
Thud.

[P83]
Her skull rang, but she did not wake up. The afterlife it was.

[P84]
Besides, that White Tiger floating there with only its upper body showing looked familiar.

[P85]
*That’s the one.*

[P86]
Snow-white fur that could almost be called silver. Blue-white eyes.

[P87]
It was the White Tiger that Young Palace Lord Yayul Mok treasured.

[P88]
Muyaho should have been dead. Yet here it was without a scratch, calmly tilting its head at her. Yohi was certain now: she was in the afterlife.

[P89]
*No wonder there’s no exit.*

[P90]
How was she supposed to know? She had never been here before.

[P91]
It felt as though a hopelessly tangled thread had finally come loose. With that moment of enlightenment, Yohi’s shoulders began to shake.

[P92]
“Sniff… You fucking bastard, Heugung…”

[P93]
The crisis facing Nanman? Her dignity as Great Chieftain of the Yao people?

[P94]
What did any of that matter? She was dead.

[P95]
The only one watching her was a half-severed tiger ghost. Then she thought of her mother, who had died twenty years ago, and tears poured down her face.

[P96]
“Waaah! Waaaaah!”

[P97]
At her cries, which sounded almost like a wild beast’s roar, Muyaho approached with a look that seemed to ask if she was one of its own kind. It licked away her tears.

[P98]
—Grrr.

[P99]
A rough tongue swept across her whole face.

[P100]
Her senses did seem awfully vivid for a ghost. Then again, anyone who claimed the dead could not feel anything had probably never been to the afterlife either.

[P101]
Yohi buried her face in Muyaho’s soft fur and wept.

[P102]
Until something soft and swishing brushed against her hand.

[P103]
Grab.

[P104]
—Hiss!

[P105]
At first, she was too busy crying to notice. Then she wondered what she had caught.

[P106]
At Muyaho’s sharp cry, she raised her head and saw the long, snow-white tail in her hand.

[P107]
*Oh. It’s a tail. For a moment, I thought…*

[P108]
Yohi buried her face in the fur again. A moment later, she lifted her head.

[P109]
One fact had hit her like a blow to the back of the head.

[P110]
*Wait. Why does it have a tail?*

[P111]
Ordinarily, that would not have been strange. Tigers had tails. Even the rats infesting the Western Yao Estate’s storerooms had tails.

[P112]
But moments ago, this White Tiger ghost had been floating there with only its upper body visible. Now it was whole.

[P113]
*Could it be?*

[P114]
Yohi sprang up and reached for the wall where Muyaho had first appeared.

[P115]
Tap.

[P116]
It was cold and hard, just as before. She could not guess its thickness, and she saw no gap.

[P117]
Still, she was not ready to give up.

[P118]
*There’s something I don’t understand. There has to be.*

[P119]
With her composure returning, reason told her this was neither a dream nor the afterlife. It was something strange—something the human mind could not easily make sense of.

[P120]
As though it had read her thoughts, Muyaho stopped circling her and moved.

[P121]
—Grrrr.

[P122]
The massive White Tiger bent its hind legs to one side. Yohi caught a hint of meaning in its clear blue-white eyes.

[P123]
“You want me to get on your back?”

[P124]
—Grrr.

[P125]
“Hah.”

[P126]
She had heard it was intelligent. She had not realized just how intelligent.

[P127]
Yohi studied Muyaho with fresh amazement, then carefully climbed onto its back. When she gripped its white fur, it stretched a huge forepaw toward the wall.

[P128]
Step.

[P129]
One stride brought them right up against the stone. Yohi squeezed her eyes shut.

[P130]
*Please.*

[P131]
The plea had barely formed when—

[P132]
Swoooosh!

[P133]
A strange sensation swept through her, as though she were being pulled somewhere. Yohi slowly opened her eyes.

[P134]
“Ah.”

[P135]
It was bright. Warm.

[P136]
Light instead of darkness. Living trees instead of cold stone. Flowers of every kind in place of vines.

[P137]
An entirely new world lay before her. For a moment, its peace and beauty made her forget everything else.

[P138]
“W-What is this place…?”

[P139]
Her question trailed off. This time, Muyaho gave no answer.

[P140]
The white tiger shot down a path lined with plants and flowers without a moment’s hesitation.

[P141]
Tap-tap. Swoooosh!

[P142]
Cool wind swept over her as the scenery raced past. Animals of every shape and color watched them with curious eyes.

[P143]
Mountain birds nested in impossibly tall trees. A roe deer and a wild boar basked together amid the thick grass. There was even a bear letting the mismatched pair lean against its body.

[P144]
*What in the world did I just see?*

[P145]
The thought vanished almost as soon as it came.

[P146]
Why did none of the animals seem to care about the food chain? She did not know. It did not matter.

[P147]
Here, simply by being in this place, everything felt natural.

[P148]
*This is… This is impossible.*

[P149]
The words *dark arts* flashed through her mind.

[P150]
Then the path that had seemed to go on forever ended at a small pond.

[P151]
And there was someone beside it.

[P152]
“Jin Taekyung!”

[P153]
It was him.

[P154]
His muscular build and the red armor over his upper body were unmistakable even from a distance. He lay collapsed, half-submerged in the clear water.

[P155]
Only a little over ten zhang separated them. But despite Yohi’s urgency, Muyaho, which had run without stopping until now, stood rooted to the spot.

[P156]
—Grrrr.

[P157]
Its low growl sounded as though it were calling to someone.

[P158]
Yohi sensed something and turned to follow its blue-white gaze.

[P159]
She saw it.

[P160]
No—she felt it before she saw it.

[P161]
Swoooosh.

[P162]
A cool wind carrying an unfamiliar qi stirred the leaves of a tree larger than any she had ever seen. Green leaves rained down.

[P163]
And then—

[P164]
Rustle.

[P165]
Beneath the vast shade of the great tree, a Black Tiger as dark as the shadows rose to its feet.

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.

- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.

## Adjudicator rules

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

Do not `REPAIR` a working SOL line. Do not invent a third style because you prefer it.

For `REPAIR`, write the smallest complete replacement needed for that hunk. It must be natural English and fully source-faithful.

## Glossary

Korean **keys** are binding unless the source uses that string in a different ordinary-language sense. Glossary **English** is not a license for a calque (`presiding chair`). If SOL is a natural recast of the same sense, keep SOL.

## Output contract

Return exactly one JSON object and no Markdown fence or prose:

Reasons must name the veto, or say that SOL keeps sense and voice. Do not merely say one version is "better" or "more natural" without stating what changed.

Keep reasons brief. Do not adjudicate unchanged passages. Do not call tools.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.
